This product, commonly known by brand names such as Implanon or Nexplanon, is a small, thin plastic rod inserted under the skin to prevent pregnancy. 11. The rod gradually releases etonogestrel, a hormone similar to one naturally produced in the body, over a three-year period. 12. This medication may be less effective in women who are significantly overweight or those taking certain other medications. 13. Before the rod is placed, read the patient information leaflet provided by your pharmacist or healthcare provider. 14. Consult your doctor about the best time to schedule the insertion procedure, as they may require a pregnancy test beforehand. 15. If the rod is inserted within the first five days of your menstrual cycle, it typically begins working immediately. 16. If the rod is placed at another time in your cycle, you may need to use a non-hormonal backup birth control method (e.g., condoms, diaphragm, spermicide) for the first seven days. 17. A healthcare professional will insert the rod under the skin of your upper arm, usually in the arm you do not use for writing. 18. After placement, ensure you can feel the rod beneath your skin. 19. The insertion site will be covered with two bandages. Leave the top bandage on for 24 hours and the smaller bandage on for 3 to 5 days, as directed by your doctor. 20. The rod must be removed after three years and can be replaced if continued birth control is desired. 21. Common side effects may include nausea, stomach cramping or bloating, dizziness, headache, breast tenderness, acne, hair loss, weight gain, and vaginal irritation or discharge. 22. Pain, bruising, numbness, infection, or scarring may occur at the insertion site. 23. Menstrual periods may become irregular, with changes in timing, duration, or flow. Spotting between periods is also common, especially during the first few months of use. 24. If bleeding is prolonged (lasting more than eight days) or unusually heavy, contact your doctor. 25. This medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. 26. Rarely, serious and potentially fatal complications from blood clots (e.g., heart attack, stroke, clots in the lungs, legs, or eyes) have been reported. 27. Severe allergic reactions to this medication are rare. 28. This is not an exhaustive list of possible side effects. In the U.S., contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for similar guidance. 29. Before using etonogestrel, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, other progestins (e.g., norethindrone, desogestrel), anesthetics, antiseptics, or any other substances. 30. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. 31. This medication may cause dizziness. Alcohol or marijuana (cannabis) can exacerbate this effect. Avoid driving, operating machinery, or performing tasks requiring alertness until you can do so safely. 32. Limit your consumption of alcoholic beverages. 33. This medication may cause blotchy, dark areas on the skin (melasma), which can worsen with sun exposure. Limit your time in the sun, and avoid tanning booths and sunlamps. 34. If you are nearsighted or wear contact lenses, you may experience vision problems or difficulty wearing your lenses. 35. This product must not be used during pregnancy. If you become pregnant or suspect you may be pregnant, inform your doctor immediately. 36. This medication can pass into breast milk. 37. Drug interactions may alter the effectiveness of this medication or increase the risk of serious side effects. 38. Keep a list of all the products you use (including prescription, non-prescription, and herbal products) and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. 39. Certain drugs may reduce the effectiveness of hormonal birth control by decreasing hormone levels in the body, potentially leading to pregnancy. Examples include griseofulvin, modafinil, rifamycins (e.g., rifampin, rifabutin), ritonavir, and St. John’s Wort. 40. Discuss with your doctor whether you should use a reliable backup birth control method when starting any new medication. 41. This medication may interfere with certain laboratory tests, such as those measuring sex-hormone-binding globulin or thyroid function, potentially causing inaccurate results. 42.
